  "title": "Composing Static and Contextual Corrections for Activation Sparsity in SwiGLU LLMs via Output-Distribution Distillation",
  "core_problem": "Training-free activation sparsity methods (WINA, TEAL, R-Sparse) have enabled 40-60% model-level neuron pruning on native SwiGLU LLMs, but leave a substantial quality gap: at 50% model-level activation sparsity on Llama-3-8B, WINA achieves 59.57% average across six standard benchmarks (PIQA, ARC-c, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, MMLU, GSM8K) versus the dense model's 66.38% — a 6.81-point drop, with reasoning-heavy tasks (GSM8K, MMLU) degrading disproportionately. Two recent learned approaches partially address this gap from complementary but individually incomplete directions. SPON (Resting Neurons, arXiv 2512.12744v3, ICML 2026 per arXiv metadata updated on the April 30 notification date) introduces static, input-independent learnable bias vectors trained via KL-divergence distillation, recovering ~1 point over WINA on five QA benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, BoolQ, PIQA, Winogrande; 71.96 vs 70.97 weighted average) at zero inference overhead — demonstrating that output-distribution alignment helps, but leaving input-dependent importance patterns entirely unaddressed. FastForward (arXiv 2602.00397) trains contextual predictors with weighted BCE loss plus an error compensation network (2-layer MLP, r'=d_model/8) trained with MSE loss that operates at inference time, achieving MMLU 67.17 vs dense 67.84 at 50% FFN sparsity on Llama-3.1-8B — demonstrating that contextual prediction helps, but requiring the auxiliary compensation network to address the output-quality deficiency inherent in BCE's per-neuron objective. The compensation network adds ~8.0 MB of weights per layer (r'=d_model/8=512; two matrices of 4096×512, totaling 4,194,304 params × 2 bytes FP16 ≈ 8.0 MB) and associated GEMV operations at inference time — substantial overhead that motivates seeking training objectives that eliminate the need for compensation entirely. The critical insight is that BCE's training signal decomposes as L_BCE = Σ_j l(y_j, s_j), a mean-field factorization P(y_1,...,y_D) ≈ Π_j P(y_j) that treats each neuron's activation decision as independent of all others. This cannot capture joint interaction effects — the fact that pruning neuron A may only degrade output quality when neuron B in the same or subsequent layer is also pruned. FastForward's error compensation network is an engineering fix for this fundamental limitation: it patches output errors post-hoc rather than training the predictor to avoid them. KL divergence on output logits, by contrast, backpropagates through the full sparse forward pass via ∂L_KL/∂θ = ∂L_KL/∂p_sparse · ∂p_sparse/∂h_out · ∂h_out/∂m · ∂m/∂θ, where the term ∂h_out/∂m captures how each neuron's mask decision jointly affects the output in combination with all other active neurons. This yields a testable prediction: KL's advantage over BCE should increase with sparsity level, because higher sparsity creates more simultaneous neuron removals and thus more pairwise and higher-order interaction terms that BCE's independent decomposition cannot model. A further open question is whether learned sparsity predictors trained on short calibration sequences generalize to long-context settings — SVD Contextual Sparsity Predictors (arXiv 2603.14110) explicitly found that learned predictors suffer from out-of-distribution sensitivity compared to weight-structure-based approaches, making long-context evaluation essential for any learned predictor method.",
  "opportunity": "The landscape reveals four actionable opportunities. First, the composition question: SPON's static bias correction fixes average-case representational drift (input-independent) while contextual prediction handles per-input variation (input-dependent) — orthogonal mechanisms that should provide additive benefits. If confirmed empirically, the SPON + contextual predictor composition becomes a practical recipe with a clear mechanistic explanation. Second, the training objective question: if a KL-trained predictor (no compensation) matches or exceeds the quality of FastForward's full BCE + compensation system, the practical benefit is substantial — a simpler inference pipeline with lower overhead. FastForward's compensation MLP adds ~8.0 MB of weights per layer (r'=d_model/8=512; 4,194,304 params in FP16) and associated GEMV operations at inference time — ~256 MB total across 32 layers; eliminating it simplifies deployment without sacrificing quality. This transforms the contribution from 'KL is slightly better than BCE' to 'KL training makes error compensation unnecessary.' Third, the formal mean-field analysis elevates the contribution from empirical observation to principled insight: we derive that BCE's per-neuron decomposition L_BCE = Σ_j l(y_j, s_j) is equivalent to optimizing under a mean-field factorized posterior over neuron importance, ignoring all pairwise and higher-order interaction terms. At sparsity level s, the number of simultaneously pruned neuron pairs scales as O(s²D²), so the approximation gap grows quadratically with sparsity — predicting that KL's advantage should be substantially larger at 50% than at 40% sparsity. This is a testable, falsifiable prediction that, if confirmed, provides actionable guidance for all future predictor design. Fourth, long-context generalization: learned sparsity predictors are trained on short calibration sequences, but deployed on inputs of arbitrary length. SVD Contextual Sparsity Predictors (arXiv 2603.14110) showed that learned predictors exhibit out-of-distribution sensitivity — our LongBench and MT-Bench evaluation directly tests whether KL-trained predictors (which optimize for output-distribution preservation rather than per-neuron pattern matching) exhibit better generalization than BCE-trained ones, and whether SPON's static correction provides a context-length-invariant baseline that stabilizes long-context performance. The contribution is fivefold: (1) the first empirical study of whether static bias correction (SPON) and contextual prediction compose additively for activation sparsity — the headline result; (2) a controlled four-condition ablation (BCE, BCE+compensation, KL, KL+compensation) testing whether KL training subsumes error compensation; (3) a formalized mean-field argument with the sparsity-level interaction prediction; (4) a systematic three-tier comparison (training-free, static-learned, contextual-learned) on native SwiGLU at decode time with honest wall-clock overhead reporting; and (5) long-context generalization evaluation testing whether learned predictors trained on short sequences maintain quality on LongBench tasks (4K-32K tokens), addressing a gap identified by recent work on predictor OOD sensitivity.",
  "landscape": "Training-free activation sparsity on SwiGLU has rapidly progressed: WINA (ICLR 2026) achieves the training-free SOTA with weight-informed scoring and greedy per-layer sparsity allocation across both MLP and attention layers (with attention tolerating ~2.3× higher sparsity than MLP), reporting 59.57% average on Llama-3-8B at 50% model-level sparsity versus 66.38% dense; WAS (EMNLP 2025) achieves 60% model-level sparsity via weight-aware scoring with constrained Bayesian optimization; WiSparse (arXiv 2026) preserves 97% of dense performance at 50% sparsity via weight-aware mixed-granularity allocation; TEAL (ICLR 2025) achieves 40-50% sparsity with 1.5-1.8x speedup via magnitude pruning; R-Sparse (ICLR 2025) achieves 50% model-level sparsity via rank-aware input channel scoring; ActTail (arXiv 2026) uses Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization for global sparsity allocation; DIP (MLSys 2025) achieves predictor-free dynamic pruning on SwiGLU at ~40% speedup plus LoRA adapters trained via KL-distillation for accuracy recovery — the closest existing system combining KL-distillation with sparsity, though critically it trains the LoRA recovery module with KL rather than the sparsity predictor itself, and uses magnitude-based (not predicted) sparsity masks. On the learned side, SPON/Resting Neurons (arXiv 2512.12744v3, ICML 2026 per arXiv metadata updated on the April 30 notification date) injects learnable input-independent activation vectors trained via KL-divergence distillation, recovering ~1 point over WINA at 50% model-level sparsity on five QA benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, BoolQ, PIQA, Winogrande; 71.96 vs 70.97), with zero inference overhead since vectors fold into bias terms, training in ~1 hour on 4x A6000; SPON also reports perplexity on WikiText and validates cross-dataset generalization by calibrating on C4 while evaluating on WikiText. FastForward (arXiv 2602.00397, Jan 2026) trains a contextual predictor (single-head attention + 2-layer MLP, bottleneck r=d_model/16) with weighted BCE loss plus an error compensation network (2-layer MLP, r'=d_model/8=512) trained with MSE loss ||Y_dense − Y_sparse||², achieving MMLU 67.17 vs dense 67.84 at 50% FFN sparsity on Llama-3.1-8B — critically, the compensation network operates at inference time (not just training), adding ~8.0 MB per layer (4,194,304 params × 2 bytes FP16, ~256 MB total across 32 layers) in per-layer weight reads and compute overhead. FastForward targets prefill optimization and evaluates on LongBench (English tasks, 4K-32K tokens) achieving <6% accuracy loss at 50% FFN sparsity — demonstrating that their predictor generalizes beyond short training sequences via an attention-mixing mechanism, but requiring the compensation network for this generalization. ShadowLLM (EMNLP 2024) trains single-hidden-layer predictors using MSE loss on per-neuron importance. Sirius (NeurIPS 2024) addresses quality degradation from contextual sparsity via periodic full-model correction every 16 tokens with speculative-decoding-style rollback, achieving 20-35% latency reduction — a complementary approach to our static+contextual composition since Sirius interleaves sparse and dense inference rather than composing learned correction mechanisms. Spark Transformer (NeurIPS 2025) reparameterizes existing FFN weights and attention key embeddings during pre-training (Gemma-2 recipe) to form implicit sparsity predictors with a hardware-friendly 'statistical top-k' linear-time approximate algorithm, achieving 2.5x FLOP reduction with 1.79x CPU / 1.40x GPU decode speedup and only 8% of FFN neurons activated — complementary to our post-training approach which works on frozen models without pre-training modification. ActiveFlow (arXiv 2025) combines cross-layer preloading with sparse-aware self-distillation using KL-divergence to adapt model weights (not predictor parameters) for on-device deployment, demonstrating that KL-based training recovers 2.64-10.21% accuracy over TEAL — further evidence that output-distribution distillation is effective for sparsity recovery, though applied to weight adaptation rather than predictor training. Polar Sparsity (NeurIPS 2025) trained BCE routers and evaluated on LongBench for instruction-tuned models, concluding MLP sparsity offers limited benefits on SwiGLU in batch-scaling scenarios — however, this was with activation-pattern prediction, not output-distribution alignment in low-batch decode; their long-context evaluation was limited to 16K tokens. MaskLLM (NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight) uses Gumbel Softmax for static 2:4 masks. SDMPrune (arXiv 2025) uses self-distillation for MLP weight pruning, not activation sparsity. SVD Contextual Sparsity Predictors (arXiv 2603.14110, Mar 2026) provide training-free predictors using truncated SVD of gate projections, targeting ReGLU-based models with high inherent sparsity — critically, they found that learned predictors suffer from out-of-distribution sensitivity on unseen data (ROC-AUC degrades on held-out sequences) while SVD predictors maintain robust performance by leveraging weight structure rather than data-dependent patterns. This OOD sensitivity finding directly motivates our LongBench evaluation: if learned predictors are fragile to distribution shift, their behavior on long-context tasks (absent from short calibration data) is an important empirical question. No prior work (a) trains the sparsity predictor itself with KL-divergence distillation, (b) tests whether SPON's static correction composes additively with contextual prediction, (c) formally analyzes BCE's mean-field limitation and its interaction with sparsity level, or (d) evaluates whether KL-trained predictors generalize better than BCE-trained ones on long-context tasks.",
  "approach": "We study the composition of two learned correction mechanisms for activation sparsity — static bias correction and contextual prediction — trained via output-distribution distillation (KL divergence) on native SwiGLU LLMs at decode time, with a controlled four-condition ablation testing whether KL training subsumes error compensation. For each SwiGLU MLP block in Llama 3.1 8B (32 layers, d_model=4096, intermediate_size=14336), we attach a low-rank predictor that maps the layer input hidden state h ∈ R^d to a continuous sparsity score over the intermediate dimension D via two linear projections: h → W_down (4096 × 128) → ReLU → W_up (128 × 14336), yielding ~2.36M parameters per layer (~75.5M total, <1% of 8B model). Architecture is fixed at rank r=128 (no rank sweep, following reviewer guidance to narrow scope). During training, scores are converted to differentiable binary masks via Gumbel-sigmoid relaxation with temperature annealing (τ: 5 → 0.1). The primary training loss is: L = KL(p_dense || p_sparse) + λ_mse · MSE(h_dense_l, h_sparse_l) + λ_sparse · max(0, s − s_target), where KL divergence on output logits is the primary signal (capturing joint neuron interactions through end-to-end gradient flow via ∂L_KL/∂θ = ∂L_KL/∂p_sparse · ∂p_sparse/∂h_out · ∂h_out/∂m · ∂m/∂θ), per-layer MSE provides gradient signal for early layers, and the sparsity penalty enforces target model-level sparsity s_target = 0.5. Only predictor parameters are updated during ~1K gradient steps on SlimPajama calibration data with the base LLM frozen. MLP/attention sparsity allocation: We follow WINA's greedy per-layer allocation algorithm (originally from TEAL) to distribute the 50% global FLOPs budget across all layers. This algorithm iteratively increases sparsity in the least-sensitive layer (measured by calibration perplexity impact) until the aggregate meets the global target. WINA found that attention layers tolerate ~2.3× higher sparsity than MLP layers, so the allocation typically assigns ~55-65% sparsity to attention layers and ~40-50% to MLP layers, though the exact per-layer ratios are determined by the calibration-based optimization. Within MLP layers, our contextual predictor replaces WINA's heuristic scoring to determine which neurons to activate; within attention layers, WINA's original weight-informed scoring is used unchanged. We report both the global model-level sparsity (50%) and the effective per-component (MLP, attention) sparsity ratios resulting from the allocation, ensuring transparent comparison with baselines that may use different allocation strategies. At inference, the predictor produces a binary mask via top-k selection, and the sparse SwiGLU forward pass skips columns of gate/up projections and rows of the down projection using Triton sparse GEMV kernels from the TEAL/WINA codebases. Predictor overhead — FLOPs and wall-clock (honest reporting): Each predictor adds ~4.72M FLOPs per layer (two GEMVs of 4096×128 and 128×14336) versus ~176M FLOPs saved at 50% MLP sparsity — a ~37:1 FLOPs ratio. However, batch=1 decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound. On H100 (3.35 TB/s peak HBM bandwidth), the small predictor GEMVs achieve only ~100 GB/s effective bandwidth due to low matrix occupancy and kernel launch overhead, yielding ~0.047 ms per layer or ~1.5 ms total predictor overhead across 32 layers. The larger FFN matrices being skipped achieve ~500 GB/s effective bandwidth, yielding ~0.35 ms savings per layer or ~11.3 ms total savings. The realistic wall-clock savings-to-overhead ratio is approximately 4-8:1 — still attractive for decode acceleration, but substantially lower than the 37:1 FLOPs ratio. We report both metrics throughout to avoid misleading claims. Four-condition ablation (the key experimental design addition): (a) BCE only — our predictor architecture trained with weighted BCE loss (FastForward-style exponential weighting), no compensation; (b) BCE + error compensation — same BCE predictor plus FastForward's 2-layer compensation MLP (r'=d_model/8=512, adding ~8.0 MB per layer: W_comp1 ∈ R^{4096×512} + W_comp2 ∈ R^{512×4096} = 4,194,304 params × 2 bytes FP16), trained with MSE loss ||Y_dense − (Y_sparse + g_φ(h))||², with compensation network active at inference time; (c) KL only — our predictor trained with KL-divergence loss, no compensation; (d) KL + error compensation — if time permits. Condition (b) is critical: it replicates FastForward's full approach (BCE + compensation) rather than testing BCE in isolation, ensuring a fair comparison. If KL-only (c) matches or exceeds BCE+compensation (b), the finding is that KL training makes error compensation unnecessary — yielding a simpler system with lower inference overhead (eliminating ~256 MB of compensation weights and associated compute across 32 layers). Evaluation benchmarks (aligned with user requirements): (1) Perplexity on WikiText-2 and C4 — standard for sparsity papers, reported by SPON and most training-free baselines, trivial to compute; (2) ARC-Challenge — science reasoning; (3) WinoGrande — coreference resolution; (4) MMLU — multitask knowledge; (5) GSM8K — mathematical reasoning; (6) HumanEval — code generation; (7) MT-Bench — multi-turn instruction-following quality under sparsity, evaluated using GPT-4 as judge (80 questions, 8 categories), testing whether sparsity disproportionately degrades open-ended generation; (8) LongBench (English subset) — long-context evaluation (4K-32K tokens) testing predictor generalization beyond training distribution, directly comparable to FastForward's LongBench results. This benchmark set covers all user-required evaluation axes: perplexity, knowledge/reasoning (MMLU, ARC-c, GSM8K), code (HumanEval), long-context (LongBench), and instruction-following (MT-Bench). Long-context generalization: The predictor is trained on SlimPajama calibration sequences (typically 2048 tokens). LongBench tasks require processing 4K-32K token inputs, testing whether learned neuron importance patterns generalize beyond the training context length. SVD Contextual Sparsity Predictors (arXiv 2603.14110) found that learned predictors suffer OOD sensitivity on unseen data, making this a plausible failure mode. If long-context performance degrades disproportionately, this is itself a finding — motivating context-length-aware predictor training or hybrid approaches where static SPON correction (which is context-length-invariant by construction) provides a robust baseline while contextual prediction adapts to input-specific patterns. FastForward reports their predictor generalizes to LongBench via an attention-mixing mechanism; our four-condition ablation will reveal whether KL-trained predictors (which optimize output-distribution preservation) exhibit different generalization characteristics than BCE-trained ones (which optimize per-neuron pattern accuracy). Experiments focus on Llama 3.1 8B at 50% model-level sparsity as the primary operating point. For the KL-BCE sparsity interaction test, we additionally train KL and BCE predictors at 40% model-level sparsity (2 extra training runs) to test the mean-field prediction that KL's advantage over BCE grows with sparsity level. All other baselines and the composition experiment are evaluated at 50% only, saving ~3-4 days versus evaluating at both levels. Baselines use consistent model-level sparsity: training-free baselines are WINA, TEAL, and R-Sparse; learned baselines are SPON (reimplemented — bias vectors + KL training, architecturally trivial, validated by reproducing Table 2 numbers on Llama 3 8B before evaluating on Llama 3.1 8B) and the four-condition ablation above. Key experiments ordered by importance: (1) SPON + KL predictor composition (headline): apply SPON bias correction AND contextual KL prediction simultaneously, testing whether static correction (fixing average-case drift) and contextual prediction (handling per-input variation) provide additive benefits. (2) KL-only vs BCE+compensation: the critical test of whether end-to-end KL training subsumes the need for error compensation — if confirmed, this is the key practical recommendation (eliminating ~256 MB of compensation weights and per-layer GEMV overhead). (3) KL vs BCE sparsity-level interaction: testing at both 40% and 50% whether KL's advantage over BCE (both without compensation) grows with sparsity, confirming the mean-field prediction. (4) Three-tier comparison: training-free (WINA, TEAL, R-Sparse) vs static-learned (SPON) vs contextual-learned (ours), establishing marginal value of each tier. (5) Long-context generalization: LongBench evaluation across all conditions, testing whether KL-trained predictors generalize better than BCE-trained ones to long contexts, and whether SPON's static correction stabilizes long-context performance. (6) Per-task analysis: decompose improvements by benchmark type (perplexity vs knowledge/reasoning vs code vs long-context vs instruction-following). Improvement target: 1.5-3 points average recovery over WINA at 50% model-level sparsity (WINA baseline: 59.57 on 6 benchmarks), conservatively grounded in: SPON's ~1 point static recovery (verified on five QA benchmarks), contextual KL prediction contributing an estimated 0.5-1.5 points (conservative — FastForward's near-dense MMLU quality was achieved at FFN-only sparsity with error compensation, a less aggressive operating point than our model-level sparsity without compensation), and a potential 0-0.5 point composition bonus. The 1.5-3 point range is arithmetically consistent: 1 (SPON) + 0.5-1.5 (contextual) + 0-0.5 (composition) = 1.5-3 points total. Explicit fallbacks: (A) If composition shows no additive benefit (SPON + predictor ≈ predictor alone), the contribution becomes the finding that contextual prediction subsumes static correction. (B) If KL-only does not beat BCE+compensation, the contribution pivots to the formalized mean-field analysis + three-tier comparison with the finding that error compensation remains necessary, but KL should be used in conjunction. (C) If KL does not outperform BCE at any sparsity level, the contribution becomes the rigorous negative result plus the composition study. (D) If long-context performance degrades substantially, the contribution includes the finding that predictor-based sparsity requires context-length-aware training, with SPON's static correction serving as a context-length-invariant safety net.",

  "description": "We study whether two learned correction mechanisms for activation sparsity — static bias correction and contextual prediction — address orthogonal failure modes and compose additively when both are trained via output-distribution distillation, and whether KL-divergence training for the contextual predictor subsumes the need for error compensation networks. The activation sparsity landscape has stratified into three tiers: training-free heuristics (WINA, TEAL, R-Sparse) achieving 59.57% average on Llama-3-8B at 50% model-level sparsity versus 66.38% dense (6.81-point gap); static learned correction (SPON, ICML 2026 per arXiv metadata) training input-independent bias vectors via KL-distillation, recovering ~1 point on five QA benchmarks at zero overhead; and contextual learned prediction (FastForward, arXiv 2026) training input-dependent predictors with weighted BCE plus an inference-time error compensation MLP adding ~8.0 MB per layer (~256 MB total across 32 layers). No prior work combines contextual prediction with KL-divergence distillation for the predictor itself, tests static+contextual composition, formally analyzes why BCE's per-neuron objective requires error compensation, or evaluates whether KL-trained predictors generalize better than BCE-trained ones to long-context settings. Our key theoretical contribution formalizes BCE's limitation as a mean-field factorization: L_BCE = Σ_j l(y_j, s_j) treats neuron activation decisions as independent, ignoring joint interaction effects that grow quadratically with sparsity level O(s²D²). KL divergence on output logits captures these interactions through end-to-end gradient flow (∂h_out/∂m couples all mask decisions), yielding a testable prediction: KL's advantage over BCE grows with sparsity. We test this with a controlled four-condition ablation (BCE-only, BCE+compensation, KL-only, KL+compensation) — the critical test being whether KL-only matches BCE+compensation, which would mean KL training makes error compensation unnecessary (simpler system, ~256 MB less inference overhead). Each rank-128 predictor (~2.36M params per layer, <1% of model) maps layer inputs to neuron masks via Gumbel-sigmoid relaxation. MLP/attention sparsity allocation follows WINA's greedy per-layer algorithm: at 50% global FLOPs budget, attention layers receive ~55-65% sparsity while MLP layers receive ~40-50%, with exact per-layer ratios determined by calibration-based optimization; we report both global and per-component effective sparsity.   "core_problem": "Training-free activation sparsity methods (WINA, TEAL, R-Sparse) have enabled 40-60% model-level neuron pruning on native SwiGLU LLMs, but leave a substantial quality gap: at 50% model-level activation sparsity on Llama-3-8B, WINA achieves 59.57% average across six standard benchmarks (PIQA, ARC-c, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, MMLU, GSM8K) versus the dense model's 66.38% — a 6.81-point drop, with reasoning-heavy tasks (GSM8K, MMLU) degrading disproportionately. FastForward (arXiv 2602.00397) trains contextual predictors with weighted BCE loss plus an error compensation network (2-layer MLP, r'=d_model/8) trained with MSE loss that operates at inference time, achieving MMLU 67.17 vs dense 67.84 at 50% FFN sparsity on Llama-3.1-8B — demonstrating that contextual prediction helps, but requiring the auxiliary compensation network to address the output-quality deficiency inherent in BCE's per-neuron objective. The critical insight is that BCE's training signal decomposes as L_BCE = Σ_j l(y_j, s_j), a mean-field factorization P(y_1,...,y_D) ≈ Π_j P(y_j) that treats each neuron's activation decision as independent of all others. This cannot capture joint interaction effects — the fact that pruning neuron A may only degrade output quality when neuron B in the same or subsequent layer is also pruned. FastForward's error compensation network is an engineering fix for this fundamental limitation: it patches output errors post-hoc rather than training the predictor to avoid them. KL divergence on output logits, by contrast, backpropagates through the full sparse forward pass via ∂L_KL/∂θ = ∂L_KL/∂p_sparse · ∂p_sparse/∂h_out · ∂h_out/∂m · ∂m/∂θ, where the term ∂h_out/∂m captures how each neuron's mask decision jointly affects the output in combination with all other active neurons. This yields a testable prediction: KL's advantage over BCE should increase with sparsity level, because higher sparsity creates more simultaneous neuron removals and thus more pairwise and higher-order interaction terms that BCE's independent decomposition cannot model. A further open question is whether learned sparsity predictors trained on short calibration sequences generalize to long-context settings — SVD Contextual Sparsity Predictors (arXiv 2603.14110) explicitly found that learned predictors suffer from out-of-distribution sensitivity compared to weight-structure-based approaches, making long-context evaluation essential for any learned predictor method.",
  "opportunity": "The landscape reveals four actionable opportunities. First, the composition question: SPON's static bias correction fixes average-case representational drift (input-independent) while contextual prediction handles per-input variation (input-dependent) — orthogonal mechanisms that should provide additive benefits. If confirmed empirically, the SPON + contextual predictor composition becomes a practical recipe with a clear mechanistic explanation. FastForward's compensation MLP adds ~8.0 MB of weights per layer (r'=d_model/8=512; 4,194,304 params in FP16) and associated GEMV operations at inference time — ~256 MB total across 32 layers; eliminating it simplifies deployment without sacrificing quality. This is a testable, falsifiable prediction that, if confirmed, provides actionable guidance for all future predictor design.   "landscape": "Training-free activation sparsity on SwiGLU has rapidly progressed: WINA (ICLR 2026) achieves the training-free SOTA with weight-informed scoring and greedy per-layer sparsity allocation across both MLP and attention layers (with attention tolerating ~2.3× higher sparsity than MLP), reporting 59.57% average on Llama-3-8B at 50% model-level sparsity versus 66.38% dense; WAS (EMNLP 2025) achieves 60% model-level sparsity via weight-aware scoring with constrained Bayesian optimization; WiSparse (arXiv 2026) preserves 97% of dense performance at 50% sparsity via weight-aware mixed-granularity allocation; TEAL (ICLR 2025) achieves 40-50% sparsity with 1.5-1.8x speedup via magnitude pruning; R-Sparse (ICLR 2025) achieves 50% model-level sparsity via rank-aware input channel scoring; ActTail (arXiv 2026) uses Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization for global sparsity allocation; DIP (MLSys 2025) achieves predictor-free dynamic pruning on SwiGLU at ~40% speedup plus LoRA adapters trained via KL-distillation for accuracy recovery — the closest existing system combining KL-distillation with sparsity, though critically it trains the LoRA recovery module with KL rather than the sparsity predictor itself, and uses magnitude-based (not predicted) sparsity masks. MaskLLM (NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight) uses Gumbel Softmax for static 2:4 masks. SDMPrune (arXiv 2025) uses self-distillation for MLP weight pruning, not activation sparsity. SVD Contextual Sparsity Predictors (arXiv 2603.14110, Mar 2026) provide training-free predictors using truncated SVD of gate projections, targeting ReGLU-based models with high inherent sparsity — critically, they found that learned predictors suffer from out-of-distribution sensitivity on unseen data (ROC-AUC degrades on held-out sequences) while SVD predictors maintain robust performance by leveraging weight structure rather than data-dependent patterns. This OOD sensitivity finding directly motivates our LongBench evaluation: if learned predictors are fragile to distribution shift, their behavior on long-context tasks (absent from short calibration data) is an important empirical question. No prior work (a) trains the sparsity predictor itself with KL-divergence distillation, (b) tests whether SPON's static correction composes additively with contextual prediction, (c) formally analyzes BCE's mean-field limitation and its interaction with sparsity level, or (d) evaluates whether KL-trained predictors generalize better than BCE-trained ones on long-context tasks.",
  "approach": "We study the composition of two learned correction mechanisms for activation sparsity — static bias correction and contextual prediction — trained via output-distribution distillation (KL divergence) on native SwiGLU LLMs at decode time, with a controlled four-condition ablation testing whether KL training subsumes error compensation. Architecture is fixed at rank r=128 (no rank sweep, following reviewer guidance to narrow scope). During training, scores are converted to differentiable binary masks via Gumbel-sigmoid relaxation with temperature annealing (τ: 5 → 0.1). The primary training loss is: L = KL(p_dense || p_sparse) + λ_mse · MSE(h_dense_l, h_sparse_l) + λ_sparse · max(0, s − s_target), where KL divergence on output logits is the primary signal (capturing joint neuron interactions through end-to-end gradient flow via ∂L_KL/∂θ = ∂L_KL/∂p_sparse · ∂p_sparse/∂h_out · ∂h_out/∂m · ∂m/∂θ), per-layer MSE provides gradient signal for early layers, and the sparsity penalty enforces target model-level sparsity s_target = 0.5. At inference, the predictor produces a binary mask via top-k selection, and the sparse SwiGLU forward pass skips columns of gate/up projections and rows of the down projection using Triton sparse GEMV kernels from the TEAL/WINA codebases. Condition (b) is critical: it replicates FastForward's full approach (BCE + compensation) rather than testing BCE in isolation, ensuring a fair comparison. If KL-only (c) matches or exceeds BCE+compensation (b), the finding is that KL training makes error compensation unnecessary — yielding a simpler system with lower inference overhead (eliminating ~256 MB of compensation weights and associated compute across 32 layers). This benchmark set covers all user-required evaluation axes: perplexity, knowledge/reasoning (MMLU, ARC-c, GSM8K), code (HumanEval), long-context (LongBench), and instruction-following (MT-Bench). LongBench tasks require processing 4K-32K token inputs, testing whether learned neuron importance patterns generalize beyond the training context length. SVD Contextual Sparsity Predictors (arXiv 2603.14110) found that learned predictors suffer OOD sensitivity on unseen data, making this a plausible failure mode. If long-context performance degrades disproportionately, this is itself a finding — motivating context-length-aware predictor training or hybrid approaches where static SPON correction (which is context-length-invariant by construction) provides a robust baseline while contextual prediction adapts to input-specific patterns. FastForward reports their predictor generalizes to LongBench via an attention-mixing mechanism; our four-condition ablation will reveal whether KL-trained predictors (which optimize output-distribution preservation) exhibit different generalization characteristics than BCE-trained ones (which optimize per-neuron pattern accuracy). Experiments focus on Llama 3.1 8B at 50% model-level sparsity as the primary operating point. For the KL-BCE sparsity interaction test, we additionally train KL and BCE predictors at 40% model-level sparsity (2 extra training runs) to test the mean-field prediction that KL's advantage over BCE grows with sparsity level. All other baselines and the composition experiment are evaluated at 50% only, saving ~3-4 days versus evaluating at both levels. ## Overview

RULER is a synthetic benchmark with flexible configurations for customized sequence length and task complexity to provide comprehensive evaluation of long-context LMs. RULER generates synthetic examples to evaluate long-context language models with configurable sequence length and task complexity.

## Why RULER Was Created

The simple retrieval-based needle-in-a-haystack test is indicative of only a superficial form of long-context understanding. Despite achieving perfect results in the widely used needle-in-a-haystack test, almost all models fail to maintain their performance in other tasks of RULER as input length increases.

RULER introduces new task categories multi-hop tracing and aggregation to test behaviors beyond searching from context. More specifically, RULER has 13 official tasks spanning retrieval, multi-hop tracing, aggregation, and QA.

RULER expands upon the vanilla NIAH test to encompass variations with diverse types and quantities of needles. These include:
- Single NIAH where a single "needle" needs to be retrieved from the "haystack"

Variable tracking checks the behavior of tracking relevant co-occurrence patterns and drawing skipped connections within long input. content.content:
# IFPruning: Architecture and Training Analysis

## (1) Sparsity Predictor Architecture

The predictor comprises two modules:
- A lightweight 302M-parameter language model as feature extractor
- A two-layer MLP prediction head that outputs importance scores

"The last hidden state of the final input token will be used as the features of the input," then transformed through layers outputting L×d_ffn dimensions (where L is the number of LLM layers).

## (2) Training Objective

The method uses **cross-entropy loss** for next-token prediction, not KL divergence. During continued pre-training, the loss is:

"∑_{k=1}^{K-1} ∑_{x_i ∈ x^{(k+1)}} ℓ[f(x_{<i}; θ, m^{(k)}), x_i]"

Both the sparsity predictor and masked LLM are jointly optimized via this single objective.

## (3) Instruction vs. Input-Level Sparsity

The method supports both approaches:
- **Per-input masks**: Each test input generates its own pruning mask
- **Per-task masks**: A human-written task description generates one shared mask for all inputs in a dataset

This dual capability allows flexible deployment depending on use case requirements.

## (4) LLM Weight Modification

The base LLM weights are **modified during training**. The method "jointly optimizes the sparsity predictor and language model," meaning both components undergo gradient updates during continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning stages.

## (5) Sparsity Granularity

The method operates at the **FFN dimension level** (instruction-level/task-level), not token-level. It prunes "entire rows or columns of the weight matrices" in feed-forward layers, with masks applying uniformly across all tokens in a sequence.

**Models tested**: 6B, 9B, and 12B parameter LLMs pruned to activate 3B parameters each

**Evaluation benchmarks**: HumanEval, MBPP, MultiPL-E, GSM8K, MATH, MMLU, IFEval, AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard, ARC, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PiQA, and others

Architecture is fixed at rank r=128 (no rank sweep, following reviewer guidance to narrow scope). During training, scores are converted to differentiable binary masks via Gumbel-sigmoid relaxation with temperature annealing (τ: 5 → 0.1). The primary training loss is: L = KL(p_dense || p_sparse) + λ_mse · MSE(h_dense_l, h_sparse_l) + λ_sparse · max(0, s − s_target), where KL divergence on output logits is the primary signal (capturing joint neuron interactions through end-to-end gradient flow via ∂L_KL/∂θ = ∂L_KL/∂p_sparse · ∂p_sparse/∂h_out · ∂h_out/∂m · ∂m/∂θ), per-layer MSE provides gradient signal for early layers, and the sparsity penalty enforces target model-level sparsity s_target = 0.5.   "approach": "We study the composition of two learned correction mechanisms for activation sparsity — static bias correction and contextual prediction — trained via output-distribution distillation (KL divergence) on native SwiGLU LLMs at decode time, with a controlled four-condition ablation testing whether KL training subsumes error compensation. For each SwiGLU MLP block in Llama 3.1 8B (32 layers, d_model=4096, intermediate_size=14336), we attach a low-rank predictor that maps the layer input hidden state h ∈ R^d to a continuous sparsity score over the intermediate dimension D via two linear projections: h → W_down (4096 × 128) → ReLU → W_up (128 × 14336), yielding ~2.36M parameters per layer (~75.5M total, <1% of 8B model). Architecture is fixed at rank r=128 (no rank sweep, following reviewer guidance to narrow scope). During training, scores are converted to differentiable binary masks via Gumbel-sigmoid relaxation with temperature annealing (τ: 5 → 0.1). The primary training loss is: L = KL(p_dense || p_sparse) + λ_mse · MSE(h_dense_l, h_sparse_l) + λ_sparse · max(0, s − s_target), where KL divergence on output logits is the primary signal (capturing joint neuron interactions through end-to-end gradient flow via ∂L_KL/∂θ = ∂L_KL/∂p_sparse · ∂p_sparse/∂h_out · ∂h_out/∂m · ∂m/∂θ), per-layer MSE provides gradient signal for early layers, and the sparsity penalty enforces target model-level sparsity s_target = 0.5. Only predictor parameters are updated during ~1K gradient steps on SlimPajama calibration data with the base LLM frozen. MLP/attention sparsity allocation: We follow WINA's greedy per-layer allocation algorithm (originally from TEAL) to distribute the 50% global FLOPs budget across all layers. This algorithm iteratively increases sparsity in the least-sensitive layer (measured by calibration perplexity impact) until the aggregate meets the global target. WINA found that attention layers tolerate ~2.3× higher sparsity than MLP layers, so the allocation typically assigns ~55-65% sparsity to attention layers and ~40-50% to MLP layers, though the exact per-layer ratios are determined by the calibration-based optimization. Within MLP layers, our contextual predictor replaces WINA's heuristic scoring to determine which neurons to activate; within attention layers, WINA's original weight-informed scoring is used unchanged. We report both the global model-level sparsity (50%) and the effective per-component (MLP, attention) sparsity ratios resulting from the allocation, ensuring transparent comparison with baselines that may use different allocation strategies. At inference, the predictor produces a binary mask via top-k selection, and the sparse SwiGLU forward pass skips columns of gate/up projections and rows of the down projection using Triton sparse GEMV kernels from the TEAL/WINA codebases. Predictor overhead — FLOPs and wall-clock (honest reporting): Each predictor adds ~4.72M FLOPs per layer (two GEMVs of 4096×128 and 128×14336) versus ~176M FLOPs saved at 50% MLP sparsity — a ~37:1 FLOPs ratio. Condition (b) is critical: it replicates FastForward's full approach (BCE + compensation) rather than testing BCE in isolation, ensuring a fair comparison. If KL-only (c) matches or exceeds BCE+compensation (b), the finding is that KL training makes error compensation unnecessary — yielding a simpler system with lower inference overhead (eliminating ~256 MB of compensation weights and associated compute across 32 layers). Evaluation benchmarks (aligned with user requirements): (1) Perplexity on WikiText-2 and C4 — standard for sparsity papers, reported by SPON and most training-free baselines, trivial to compute; (2) ARC-Challenge — science reasoning; (3) WinoGrande — coreference resolution; (4) MMLU — multitask knowledge; (5) GSM8K — mathematical reasoning; (6) HumanEval — code generation; (7) MT-Bench — multi-turn instruction-following quality under sparsity, evaluated using GPT-4 as judge (80 questions, 8 categories), testing whether sparsity disproportionately degrades open-ended generation; (8) LongBench (English subset) — long-context evaluation (4K-32K tokens) testing predictor generalization beyond training distribution, directly comparable to FastForward's LongBench results; (9) RULER (COLM 2024) — synthetic long-context evaluation with 13 tasks across 4 categories (Retrieval including needle-in-a-haystack variants with single/multi-key/multi-value/multi-query needles, Multi-hop Tracing via variable tracking, Aggregation via common/frequent word extraction, and QA based on SQuAD/HotpotQA) at controlled context lengths (4K, 8K, 16K, 32K), using 500 examples per task with recall-based accuracy scoring.   "description": "We study whether two learned correction mechanisms for activation sparsity — static bias correction and contextual prediction — address orthogonal failure modes and compose additively when both are trained via output-distribution distillation, and whether KL-divergence training for the contextual predictor subsumes the need for error compensation networks.
